title: With David Choe and Asa Akira
summary: A Hawaii mini-show recorded by David Choe, Critter Fleming and Harry Kim while Asa Akira is away on book tour. It begins with their vacation, Harry's move from filmmaking toward accounting, sex and relationship avoidance, then asks why Harry and Critter seem happy while Choe is easily pulled toward anger and self-destruction. The answer is not a single technique: humor, food, release, friendship and deliberate social environment all appear, alongside the contradiction that cheerfulness can coexist with violence. Choe connects the lesson to an old `turkeys and eagles` diversion class, says people around him can draw out his best or worst self, and describes revenge, success, money, sex and public expression as changing but incomplete answers. A long favorite-film section maps Roadside Prophets to Thumbs Up, First Blood to his leave-me-alone childhood identification, Jodorowsky and Man Bites Dog to formal freedom, and edited-TV/Betamax memories to how films were first encountered. The apparent outro opens into a second ending about wants versus needs, the career cost of DVDASA, making the show he needed as a teenager, and David Chang's role-model challenge. Every idea and offensive passage remains. The editorial layer protects private partners and contacts, corrects public names/titles, rejects the invented David Chang substitution at 5901, and keeps named dialogue withheld.
source_notes: The cleaner removes one 24.78-second punctuation-only `. . .` span and three empty zero-duration records. It drops three whitespace tokens and no intelligible speech.

The fuzzy suggestion `did hang` → `David Chang` at 5901.48 is rejected. The complete sentence is `you also get opportunities because you did hang out with me`; David Chang is actually introduced much later at 6471.90.

KGB means Koreans Gone Bad in this recording. The episode gives the full title at 2778.28 and again at 6151.18 while discussing Harry's participation. This does not establish a global expansion for other recordings.
The catalog title mentions Asa Akira, but the opening says she is away on book tour. The audible mini-show explicitly introduces David Choe, Critter Fleming and Harry Kim.
Public-name/title repairs include Manago Hotel, Seijun Suzuki, Abbe Wool, Jodorowsky, Mœbius, Dune, Edward Norton, The Silence of the Lambs and David Chang.

AFI credits Abbe Wool as the Roadside Prophets writer-director, and the Society of Architectural Historians dates the Manago Hotel site to 1917: https://catalog.afi.com/Catalog/MovieDetails/59376 and https://sah-archipedia.org/buildings/HI-01-HA18
Sony's official Jodorowsky's Dune page confirms that the unrealized project was Dune and names Mœbius among the collaborators: https://www.sonypictures.com/movies/jodorowskysdune
Claims about crimes, money, trusts, career offers, private conversations, violence and opportunity loss remain attributed recollections rather than verified records or advice.
No diarized turns or identity windows are present in the Episode 127 artifact. Participant presence does not justify assigning each transcript line to a name.

connections.why: The absent full cast becomes a smaller location recording rather than a missed release.
A filmmaker and recurring screen presence deliberately returns to school for accounting.
No-time reasoning masks fear, maintenance and possible harm to a partner.
Recognition continues years after the road series and centers Harry's nonverbal presence.
Boarding a stranger's moored boat becomes a light example of action before reflection.
Age-of-consent jokes are preserved without making legality a complete consent standard.
Forced laughter is described as protection from dark thoughts, not medical care.
The present 80/20 joy claim is explicitly contrasted with earlier suicidal misery.
Harry's decade of filming Choe becomes a maker/subject-reversal thought experiment.
The comparison asks when a documentary's nominal subject becomes less interesting than its maker.
Critter's cheerfulness coexists with repeated stories of fights, resisting a simple good-vibes portrait.
Crying and sadness are acknowledged before the advice to stop holding on.
A juvenile diversion tape supplies the episode's vocabulary for social influence.
Friends, family and collaborators are described as drawing out different selves.
Choe says he became more, not less, susceptible to the people around him.
Travel and destructive instinct are both framed as impulses that trusted friends can slow.
Hating and repeatedly enjoying P.O.D. becomes evidence that happiness and sadness can coexist.
Success, sex and money deliver satisfaction but do not resolve the later want/need questions.
Rambo's plea to be left alone becomes Choe's metaphor for childhood abuse and retaliatory fantasy.
Edited television and Betamax changed plot comprehension and made films repeatable household objects.
The road film is named as a direct formal and social influence on Choe and Harry's series.
Their work provides a model for accessible but subversive, interpretation-demanding art.
The goal is neither pure obscurity nor bland scale, but subversion inside accessible form.
The same show made for survival is said to close television, brand and guest opportunities.
Two Korean public figures push role-model responsibility onto each other, then tease each other's compromises.
